_comment: The rung matrix, shared VERBATIM by the harness UI (harness.js fetches it) and
the Playwright suite (e2e/test_capability_ladder.py json.loads it). Same reason
caps-mask.js is one file: a harness whose rungs differ from the suite's rungs is
proving a ladder nobody ships.
ONE LADDER, top to bottom:  webgpu -> webgl2 -> webgl1 -> canvas2d -> css3d -> form.
The first five rungs are @axiom/web-engine's probed render tiers; 'form' is the
served document itself — nine <button type=submit> in a real <form method=POST>,
which needs no script and no stylesheet and is therefore the one rung nothing can
fail to reach. The page publishes where it landed on window.__axiomTier and the
whole engine report on window.__renderProbe.
A rung is named for the tier you should LAND ON, and its deny list is every tier
strictly ABOVE it — cumulative, so each rung is the previous one plus one more
denial. 'webgpu' denies nothing (the unconstrained ladder); 'css3d' denies every
rung above the terminal fail-safe. Naming rungs by their outcome rather than by
their denial is the only way a row reads as an assertion: row css3d expects tier
css3d.
'drawn' is how that rung paints, and it is checked because 'the detector said
webgl1' and 'a board actually mounted at webgl1' are different facts: engine rungs
insert a <canvas> behind the buttons, css3d builds its chests inside them, and the
form draws nothing at all.
_crossCutComment: Cross-cuts are the things a locked-down browser does that are NOT about drawing,
so the claim for almost all of them is the same and is machine-independent:
'sameTierAsBaseline' — denying this must not move the render tier at all. That is
asserted against a tier measured on THIS machine with nothing denied, so the row
means the same thing on a laptop with a GPU and on a VDI session without one.
'nativePost' says the pick leaves as a real form navigation instead of an in-place
fetch/XHR, and 'afterPickTier' is the rung the page must ADMIT to once a transport

crossCuts.label: fetch removed (XHR survives)
crossCuts.note: The transport ladder's second rung. The pick still posts in place, over XMLHttpRequest.

crossCuts.label: fetch present but always rejects
crossCuts.note: The one that ships broken: typeof fetch === 'function' is true and every request dies. Feature detection cannot see it; only a real attempt inside try/catch can. XHR carries the pick.

crossCuts.label: no fetch, no XHR
crossCuts.note: Nothing can post in place. The render tier is untouched — drawing and posting are orthogonal — and the pick falls all the way back to the form the page shipped with.

crossCuts.label: fetch rejects, XHR removed
crossCuts.note: Both transports are present-looking and both die. The page must discover it by trying, announce the drop to 'form', and re-submit natively.

crossCuts.label: WebSocket removed
crossCuts.note: A corporate proxy that allows HTTP and kills WS. Nothing here needs a socket.

crossCuts.label: WebAssembly removed
crossCuts.note: Policy-blocked wasm. This build is plain JS and must not care.

crossCuts.label: canvas readback blocked (SecurityError)
crossCuts.note: Brave farbling / Tor / a tainted canvas. The engine's control probe must notice, stop treating pixels as evidence and fall back to STRUCTURAL proof — a Tor user on a good GPU must not be dropped to css3d.

crossCuts.label: navigator.gpu present, no adapter
crossCuts.note: The faithful shape of hardware acceleration being off, and of --disable-3d-apis: presence detection says yes and only asking gets the truth.

crossCuts.label: CSS 3D flattened
crossCuts.note: preserve-3d denied AND transform-style forced flat. css3d is the terminal rung, so on a machine that reaches anything above it nothing should move at all.

launchFlags.label: WebGL2 off at the browser level (WebGL1 survives)
launchFlags.why: Measured: this kills WebGL2 and leaves WebGL1 alive — the same rung the mask reaches one layer up. The suite runs both; a disagreement is a real bug in the detection logic, not a harness artifact.

launchFlags.label: all WebGL off at the browser level
launchFlags.why: Measured: kills WebGL2 and WebGL1 both. Note that --disable-gpu does NOT do this — it falls back to SwiftShader and WebGL stays alive, so it must never be used to mean 'no GPU'.

launchFlags.label: software WebGL (SwiftShader)
launchFlags.why: The most Citrix-realistic condition: WebGL is present and entirely software-rasterized. The tier must stay webgl2 — a software rasterizer is a usable tier, not a failure.

_unenforceableInPage: Every entry in launchFlags is chosen at browser LAUNCH. A page cannot relaunch its own browser, so the harness UI can only print the command line for these — it cannot enforce them. The Playwright suite launches a browser per flag set and does enforce them.
CPU throttling (Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate, 20x) is a DevTools-protocol emulation with no in-page equivalent at all. The suite drives it over CDP.

Turning JavaScript off is enforceable in the harness ONLY through an iframe sandbox without allow-scripts — and that sandbox MUST include allow-forms, or the form POST is silently swallowed and the rung the no-JS test exists to prove is the very thing the harness deletes.

No sandbox token, CSP directive or Permissions-Policy feature exists for WebGPU, WebGL2, WebGL1, Canvas2D or CSS 3D — measured. That is why the render rungs are masked in-realm by caps-mask.js rather than by the platform.
